newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Brown reaffirms plans for unemployed.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Brown reaffirms plans for unemployed.

text.p: A Labour government would tackle unemployment in Britain by offering tax rebates to companies to take people on, shadow finance spokesman Gordon Brown said on Thursday. Brown reaffirmed that a Labour government would levy a one-off windfall tax on privatised utitilities and use three billion pounds of the revenue raised to fund its unemployment schemes.

"A tax rebate of 60 pounds a week will be offered to take young people on," Brown said in a speech for delivery to the Fabian Society. And a rebate of 75 stg will be offered to companies who employ long-term unemployed people.
But with opportunity will come responsibility, Brown said. There will be no option to remain permanently on full unemployment benefit.

"This programme begins our modernisation of the welfare state, restoring work and the work ethic to its core," he said, adding that revenue from the windfall tax would comfortably cover his jobless programme.
"If we take office this spring, we will within a matter of weeks, introduce a Labour budget which will contain the windfall tax," Brown said.
He dismissed accusations from political opponents that the tax would lead to higher prices for consumers and lower investment levels.

"There is no question, whatever a few utilities may threaten, of any regulator allowing any rise in prices because of the windfall levy. And any attempt to lower investment levels below those which are promised would of course be in breach of undertakings made."

Brown said the Conservative government's plan to scrap inheritance and capital gains taxes in the long-run were totally unjustified. "The abolition of inheritance tax and capital gains tax...unjustified by benefits to work, effort or the wider community, would bring huge benefits to a privileged few and so we oppose these Conservative proposals."
He also reaffirmed Labour's commitment to a minimum wage.

All this will be achieved within the "golden rule" that current spending will be covered by available revenues, so the ratio of government debt to GDP will be stable "on average over the economic cycle at a prudent and sensible level."
